content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'righteousness' primarily denotes right standing before God and conformity to God's own moral character and standard. Its dominant theological use, especially in Protestant tradition, is the righteousness of God credited (imputed) to believers through faith in Christ rather than earned by works — often pictured symbolically as a clean or white garment/robe that covers the sinner. It thus functions both as a legal/relational status (justification) and as an ethical quality (upright living that flows from that status).", "primary_basis": ["Genesis 15:6 (Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness)", "Habakkuk 2:4 (the righteous shall live by faith)", "Romans 1:16-17; 3:21-26 (the righteousness of God revealed and given through faith in Christ)", "Romans 4:3-8 (righteousness counted apart from works)", "2 Corinthians 5:21 (that we might become the righteousness of God in him)", "Philippians 3:9 (a righteousness not my own, but through faith in Christ)", "Isaiah 61:10 (robe of righteousness); Isaiah 64:6 (our righteousnesses as filthy rags)", "Matthew 5:6, 5:20, 6:33 (hunger for righteousness; seek first God's kingdom and righteousness)", "Ephesians 6:14 (breastplate of righteousness)", "Revelation 19:8 (fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Forensic/imputed righteousness: a legal declaration in which Christ's righteousness is credited to the believer's account (classic Reformation/Protestant reading of justification).", "basis": ["Romans 4:3-8", "Romans 5:17-19", "2 Corinthians 5:21", "Philippians 3:9"], "prominence": "dominant"}, {"meaning": "Infused/transformative righteousness: God's grace actually makes the believer inwardly righteous, so justification and sanctification are intertwined (Roman Catholic and Orthodox emphasis; Council of Trent).", "basis": ["Romans 5:5", "1 Corinthians 6:11", "James 2:21-24", "1 John 3:7 ('the one who practices righteousness is righteous')"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Ethical/behavioral righteousness: right conduct, integrity, and obedience to God's law as a lived moral quality, apart from any technical doctrine of justification (common in Old Testament wisdom and prophetic usage and in reading the Sermon on the Mount).", "basis": ["Psalm 15", "Proverbs 10-15 (righteous vs. wicked contrasts)", "Ezekiel 18:5-9", "Matthew 5:20; 6:1"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Covenant faithfulness: 'the righteousness of God' as God's own faithfulness to his covenant promises, and human righteousness as covenant membership/loyalty (New Perspective on Paul: E.P. Sanders, James Dunn, N.T. Wright).", "basis": ["Romans 3:1-5, 3:25-26 (God's righteousness as his faithfulness/justice)", "Psalm 98:2-3", "Isaiah 46:13; 51:5-8 (righteousness paralleled with salvation and faithfulness)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Righteousness as social justice: tsedaqah/dikaiosyne understood chiefly as just treatment of the poor, the vulnerable, and society at large (liberation theology and some Old Testament scholarship; in later Jewish usage tsedaqah comes to mean almsgiving).", "basis": ["Amos 5:24 (let justice roll down... righteousness like an ever-flowing stream)", "Isaiah 1:16-17; 58:6-8", "Micah 6:8", "Jeremiah 22:3, 15-16"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Christological title: righteousness personified in or identified with Christ himself ('The LORD our righteousness'), so the term symbolizes Christ as the believer's righteousness.", "basis": ["Jeremiah 23:5-6; 33:16", "1 Corinthians 1:30 (Christ... our righteousness)"], "prominence": "common"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is a genuine, widely recognizable consensus that righteousness centrally concerns right standing with God and conformity to his standard, with the garment/robe imagery (Isaiah 61:10; Revelation 19:8; cf. Zechariah 3:3-5) as its most common symbolic representation. The major fault line is not over the core meaning but over its mechanism: imputed (Protestant) vs. infused (Catholic/Orthodox) righteousness, plus the more recent scholarly debate over whether 'righteousness of God' means a status God gives or God's own covenant faithfulness (New Perspective). These are materially different but overlapping readings of a term whose lexical range (Hebrew tsedeq/tsedaqah; Greek dikaiosyne) spans legal, relational, ethical, and social-justice senses."}
